title: Operative Delivery: Instrumental Forceps, Vacuum, Caesarean Incisions, TOLAC, and Hysterectomy
subject: ss-obg
refs: Williams Obstetrics 25e Ch 29 (Operative Vaginal Delivery), Ch 30 (Cesarean Delivery and Peripartum Hysterectomy)
ACOG Practice Bulletin on Operative Vaginal Delivery
RCOG Green-top Guideline on Operative Vaginal Delivery

steps.say: Instrumental vaginal delivery requires strict fulfillment of essential prerequisites before application. The cervix must be fully dilated, membranes ruptured, maternal pelvis adequate, and the fetal presentation must be vertex with the position precisely known. Crucially, the fetal head must be engaged with the leading bony point at or below station zero, and the maternal bladder emptied.
steps.tx: Mandatory prerequisites for **operative vaginal delivery** demand a fully dilated cervix, ruptured membranes, an **engaged fetal head**, known vertex position, an emptied maternal bladder, and adequate analgesia. Performing instrumental traction on an unengaged head is strictly prohibited in modern obstetric practice.

vis.alt: Surgical instruments showing Simpson, Wrigley, and Kielland obstetric forceps.

steps.say: Obstetric guidelines classify instrumental deliveries by station. Outlet delivery requires the scalp to be visible at the introitus without separating the labia, skull at the pelvic floor, and rotation under forty five degrees. Low delivery requires the leading bony point to be at station plus two or lower. Midpelvic delivery involves station zero to plus one, while high applications are contraindicated.
steps.tx: Guidelines classify operative vaginal delivery using strict **station classification**: **outlet forceps** require the fetal scalp visible at the introitus without separating labia and skull on pelvic floor; **low forceps** require the leading bony vertex at **station +2 or lower**; and midpelvic applications involve **station 0 or +1**.

steps.say: Specific obstetric forceps designs address distinct anatomical conditions. Simpson forceps possess an elongated cephalic curve designed for moulded fetal heads in nulliparas. Elliott forceps feature a rounder cephalic curve for unmoulded heads in multiparas. Kielland forceps feature minimal pelvic curves and a sliding lock, engineered specifically for rotational delivery of deep transverse arrest.
steps.tx: Instrument selection matches fetal cranial anatomy: **Simpson forceps** feature an elongated cephalic curve suitable for moulded heads; Elliott forceps feature rounder curves for unmoulded heads; and **Kielland forceps** feature minimal pelvic curves and a sliding lock, designed specifically as **rotational forceps** for deep transverse arrest.

left.title: Kielland Rotational Forceps
points: Minimal pelvic curve allows safe axial rotation
Sliding lock corrects fetal cranial asynclitism
Indicated for deep transverse arrest and malpositions

right.title: Simpson Traction Forceps
points: Prominent pelvic curve and separated shanks
English fixed lock stabilizes parallel blades
Optimal for traction in direct occiput anterior
Safe for outlet and low non-rotational deliveries

steps.say: Vacuum extraction requires centering the suction cup precisely over the flexion point on the sagittal suture, located three centimetres anterior to the posterior fontanelle. Applying traction along the pelvic curve promotes cephalic flexion and minimal presenting diameters. Improper placement or excessive traction risks scalp lacerations, cephalohematoma, and life-threatening neonatal subgaleal hemorrhage.
steps.tx: During **vacuum extraction**, the cup must be centered directly over the **flexion point** on the sagittal suture, located **3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle**. Proper cup traction promotes flexion and autorotation, whereas improper placement or excessive traction increases the hazard of devastating neonatal **subgaleal hemorrhage**.

nodes.label: Identify flexion point: 3 cm anterior to posterior fontanelle on sagittal suture
Seat cup without entrapping maternal vaginal or cervical tissue
Raise negative pressure to 0.8 kg/cm2 (600 mmHg) during contractions
Apply traction along pelvic axis concurrent with maternal pushing efforts

steps.say: Transverse lower uterine segment hysterotomy, or Kerr incision, represents the standard surgical technique for caesarean section. The Kerr incision offers minimal blood loss, easy anatomical closure, and a low uterine scar rupture risk of zero point five to one point zero percent in subsequent pregnancies, in contrast to a classical vertical incision which carries a four to nine percent rupture risk.
steps.tx: A transverse lower uterine segment hysterotomy, or **Kerr incision**, is the global standard for caesarean delivery. It provides excellent healing with a subsequent **uterine rupture risk under 0.5 to 1.0%**, compared with a **classical incision** which carries a prohibitive **4 to 9%** rupture risk in future pregnancies.

vis.alt: Surgical exposure and transverse hysterotomy in lower segment caesarean section.

steps.say: Trial of labour after caesarean is offered to women with one prior low transverse uterine incision and no recurrent obstetric contraindications. A planned trial of labour achieves a sixty to eighty percent success rate. However, prostaglandins such as misoprostol are strictly avoided for cervical ripening or labour induction due to significantly heightened risks of uterine scar rupture.
steps.tx: A planned **TOLAC** in candidates with a single **low transverse scar** achieves an overall **success rate of 60 to 80 percent**. However, prostaglandin agents like misoprostol are strictly contraindicated for labour induction in women with prior hysterotomy scars due to an unacceptably high rate of uterine dehiscence and rupture.

left.title: Eligible TOLAC Candidates
points: One previous low transverse caesarean section
Immediate access to emergency surgical facilities
60 to 80 percent successful vaginal delivery rate

right.title: Absolute VBAC Contraindications
points: Previous classical or inverted-T hysterotomy scar
Induction using prostaglandin E1 or E2 agents

steps.say: Emergency peripartum hysterectomy is the definitive lifesaving intervention for unmanageable postpartum hemorrhage refractory to medical uterotonics, uterine balloon tamponade, and compression sutures. Placenta accreta spectrum disorders and catastrophic uterine rupture represent the most frequent surgical indications in contemporary obstetric practice.
steps.tx: **Emergency peripartum hysterectomy** serves as the definitive surgical intervention for **life-threatening haemorrhage** unresponsive to uterotonics, balloon tamponade, or vascular ligation. In modern practice, invasive **placenta accreta spectrum** disorders and catastrophic uterine rupture represent the leading indications for peripartum organ removal.

nodes.label: Severe postpartum hemorrhage refractory to uterotonics and compression sutures
Intractable bleeding from placenta accreta spectrum or uterine rupture
Rapid multidisciplinary decision for emergency peripartum hysterectomy
Perform vascular clamping of uterine arteries to arrest life-threatening hemorrhage

steps.say: When performing peripartum hysterectomy in a hemodynamically unstable patient, subtotal or supracervical hysterectomy is significantly faster and entails less dissection of the bladder and ureters. Total hysterectomy is reserved for cases where extensive lower uterine segment bleeding or invasive cervical placenta accreta precludes leaving the cervix.
steps.tx: A **subtotal hysterectomy**, or **supracervical** amputation, is preferred in hemodynamically unstable patients because it significantly shortens operative time and minimizes bladder and **ureteral injury**. However, total hysterectomy is required when morbidly adherent placenta accreta extensively involves the lower segment and cervix.
